The answer of the witness was: "Yes, I did." My colleague should not distort the facts when he is putting his questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just speaking for myself, I don't see much distortion in his question. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So it's a simple point, sir. Did you tell the investigators about the people in that other truck and it just got left out of the statement or did you just tell us for the first time today? It happens both ways.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I did say that I saw the truck in operation. It was doing the same thing I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think I'll ask you that question again. Paragraph 7: "When I returned to the school and got out of the vehicle," so now is this the first time you've gotten out of the vehicle the whole day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: The first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: The gym door was open and there was no one next to the door. I didn't go in that direction but I parked in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if you couldn't see inside the gym, how did you know or why did you think there wasn't more people to take to the execution spot?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: The door was open. The door was open and there was no one by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you could see all the way into the gym?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: There was no need for me to go there. There were no more soldiers there to tell me to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to your statement. "When I returned to the school and got out of the vehicle, I realized that I had brought a child back from the area near the railroad. I saw the child in the bodywork of the truck, holding on to the side of the TAM truck and crying. I did not see, but I suppose that one of the soldiers by the railroad must have placed the child in the truck bodywork. I told the child to get off the side of the truck, but it told me that it couldn't since it was bleeding from the leg, which I could see since the child was wearing shorts."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I didn't tell the child to get off. I told him to move away from the side so that it wouldn't fall off the truck. I didn't tell him to get off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, the child is in the actual bed of the truck where you take cargo at this point; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there any reason why the child couldn't have ridden in the cab with you on the way back from the execution site?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question, sir. The child could have been put in the cab with you; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: But it didn't. I don't know. I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, let's keep going. "This all took place at dusk and I remember well that the child remained in the bodywork of my TAM truck for at least an hour on the road in front of the school. I stopped driving, I was shaken by all that had happened." Okay. First of all, in this statement you don't describe seeing anything difficult. You don't talk about executions or going to executions. So when you say "I was shaken by all that happened" in this statement, what are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I'm talking about the tragedy. About the things I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you'll agree with me that as we've read through the report, there's no mention of taking anyone to executions or seeing any bodies or seeing anyone shot or hearing about it or thinking about it. My question is: Sir, did you not tell the investigators all this stuff then, is that why it's not in there, or did you tell them then and they just left it all out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I was sick of it. It was very difficult for me and it was very difficult for me to see the child.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You are responsible for cleaning out the back of your truck, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you find in the back of the truck when you cleaned it out after these events? It was pretty awful, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: It was awful. I didn't find anything except for the child when I came to Orahovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Any human fluids, bodily fluids, excrement, anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's keep going. "This all took place at dusk and I remember well that the child remained in the bodywork of the TAM truck for at least an hour on the road in front of the school. I stopped driving, I was shaken by all that happened." So you are telling us today that some unknown person took a child which you thought was five or six, who was in fact seven years old if it's the same child, took him from a mass execution site where he had been injured in a volley of fire, was bleeding, secreted him in the back of your truck when he could have been put in the front of the truck, so you didn't even know they were back there, you take it -- take him back to Orahovac -- you know, this is obstruction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Asked and answered, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's not an appropriate objection for cross-examination. And I'm getting to the part that I just went over, but I think the story needs to be told in toto, which he's agreed with the part that I was able to get out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's stop here. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry to have to start over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I remember he answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This question, Your Honour, I'm sorry but it has to be done in one whole. It's crucial. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, the person gets secreted into your truck, seven year old who is bleeding, from a mass execution. You go back to Orahovac, you see the seven year old child you think is five or six bleeding in the back of truck. You sit there for one hour with this bleeding seven-year-old boy in the back of your truck. Sir, it's the position of the Prosecutor that you would never have done that, you would have never allowed a seven-year-old boy to be sitting in the back of your truck where he could very well bleed to death and die in your truck. This is something that you've made up. This is something to get back at the stories you've heard around Orahovac and around Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: Nothing was made up. This is the truth. I saw it. I would thank God for not having me to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If that child had died of loss of blood in the back of your truck, you know you would have been partly responsible, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: It may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you would never let a seven-year-old bleed to death right in front of you, would you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I would not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you -- my colleague asked you many questions concerning the fact that you did not recognise anyone in Orahovac on that day. My question is: The way you felt that day, can that partly explain that you did not recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He can ask why he didn't recognise but you can't give him the answer before you ask it. He knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The persons that is -- how did you feel that day, throughout the day, and when you look back at these events, what is the feeling that comes back to you all the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I keep going back to it and I feel all broken up inside. I feel dizzy and sick. It's not easy for one to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, when we -- when you met with members of the Defence team of Drago Nikolic, was it always obvious to you that we were talking about the transport of prisoners between the school and the water point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: Are you asking me that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Okay. I will say the question over again. When you met with members of the Defence team, either myself or with Ms. Jelena Nikolic, when you signed your statement, did you know at the time that we were talking about the transport of prisoners between the school and the water point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Did you tell us what you were transporting between the school and the water point when we met?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: What did you explain to us when we met?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: Everything that is written. As it is written, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And what did you tell us about the transport of prisoners or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: I said that I drove them from Orahovac to the tap and back, but I'm not sure that I understood your question properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: That was exactly my question. I'd like to move on to just to -- and I know this is not easy for you, but again the child in the back of your truck. My colleague asked you a question about the child was hanging on to the side of the truck. Can you describe for the Judges where is the child when you first see him, is he close to you, is he deep in the truck or -- what are we talking about? Can you just describe for the Judges when you see that child where he is exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: When I went back I got off the truck to see the two who were the escorts, among the escorts. The two of them weren't there but what I saw was a child holding on to the back side and crying. I went up to him straightaway. I told the child to move away so the soldiers couldn't see him and he said he couldn't walk, that his leg hurt, and that his leg was bleeding and I saw a little blood coming from his leg. And in the meantime, the soldiers came by and Djoko arrived within the hour. They took the child from the truck and transferred him to the van and the child was driven off to Zvornik. That's all that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have one last question. And that is, my colleague suggested to you that you made up this story for getting back, he did not say at what but he said to get back at something. My question is, do you have any reason to come and testify here today and not to say the truth?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS 3DPW 10
utterances.text: No. What I'm telling you is the truth. It's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, witness, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Tribunal, I thank you for your coming to the Tribunal to give it and now you are free to go. Have a nice trip back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Documents, Mr. Bourgon, you have an IC document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, we have one document. The list was sent from my colleague to the Prosecution. This is the sketch of the school in Orahovac and the surrounding areas, and this document bears the name "plan" with 1 to 500 for the scale. And the number of the document as marked by the witness would be 3D00084, IC 217, dated 15th September 2008. And we also have the pseudonym sheet which is 3D00482. Also dated 15 September. I did not include on this the statement of the witness. I anticipated my colleague will be asking for the statement to go into evidence because he used it. If he doesn't, then I will ask that the statement goes into evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is that plan about? Is it -- are you referring to 3D84?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The plan I was referring to, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- is the plan that the witness used and that he marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you referred to the IC document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, the IC document. But now I was -- at the last part I was talking about the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: -- of the witness so it's a different thing. So there is the map -- the sketch that he marked, the pseudonym sheet, I said about those two. If my colleague does not ask for the statement to go into evidence, I will ask for that statement to go into evidence. Thank you Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. No objection to the Defence and I will ask so we are together again on allowing this 92 ter, originally, statement into evidence, but of course not as a 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So that's the only document you will tender as evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, and that's 3732 is the number I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No objection from any of the Defence? All of them will be admitted. Pseudonym sheet and the statement will be under seal. Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next witness is ready to go. I suggest, however, that maybe if we can take a short break now, then we can probably complete the second witness before we finish, just in one go, both examination-in-chief and cross-examination. It should be a short witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll leave it in your hands. You wish to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I would prefer, Mr. President. The reason is this is a -- the next witness is a 92 ter witness and we will be very short. And the Prosecution has indicated 30 minutes so it should not go over more than one hour, one hour and 15 minutes. So if we take a short break now and we come back at 12.30, we can finish the witness today before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We take a break now, 25 minutes. --- Break taken at 12.07 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Doctor. If you could kindly take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Madam Nikolic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good afternoon to the Court. Good afternoon, witness?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We have already met so I'm going to ask you some questions now with respect to your CV and some other matters and it will be recorded in the. Could you please give us your name and surname.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Vela Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of February, 1958, in Seliste, Sekovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your name has not been entered into the transcript, could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Vela, V-e-l-a, Jovicic, J-o-v-i-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your occupation is?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I'm a doctor and I specialize in the sphere of health for school children.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What education have you had?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: The faculty of medicine and I specialized in healthcare for school children.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, could I ask you to make pauses between my questions and your answers because we speak the same language, but to give the interpreters a chance to interpret what we are saying, so that everyone can follow. And so that the transcript reflects our words.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I understand, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where do you work at present?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: The health centre of Zvornik. That's where I'm employed and then I have a contract with the general hospital of Zvornik where I work on the children's ward part time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us who is the head of the pediatric department?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: It is Mrs. Koviljka Gotovac, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who the director of the Zvornik hospital was during the war, during 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you give us the name?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Jugoslav Gavric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please pause between question and answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having given a statement to the Defence team of Drago Nikolic on the 23rd of March, 2008, and after that, an addition on the 27th of May, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read both your statements in preparing for your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 90(l)[as interpreted], I'd like to read a summary of the witness statement and the additional statement made by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, proceed, but it's not pursuant to the rules itself, but according to our direct guideline. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witness is a pediatrician by profession. She specializes in the health of school children at the health centre in Zvornik. During the war, between 1993 and 1995, she work as a pediatrician in the Zvornik hospital at the children's ward there. During that time, there were four women pediatricians working in the hospital. As a doctor she was mobilised for a period of one month, during March 1995, into the Zvornik Brigade. She performed this duty as a mobilised physician for only one month because she didn't have any experience in the treatment of adults. During the war in the hospital in Zvornik and after the war, all patients without exception had proper care and attention and medical treatment provided to them by the physicians and medical staff, nurses, regardless of their nationality or religion. During the war from 1992 to 1995, at the pediatricians ward of the Zvornik hospital there were several Muslim boys who were treated there and spent most of the war there. Among those boys were the following: Adnan, who was six months when was brought to the ward and he grew up in the hospital. Another boy named Zijo who spent the entire war in the hospital, almost four years. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. President. I think if we could go into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So you expect me, when I continue, not to mention the name in open session but we'll just refer to the individual as the boy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. After the boy was given surgical treatment, he was transferred to the pediatric ward. The witness remembers that the boy, as opposed to other children, was withdrawn and found it difficult to establish communication with other people. The child and other the other children -- well, the witness and the other doctors and medical staff liked the boy and he stayed in the hospital until January 1996 when he was taken away by the Red Cross. The witness claims that during the war, including July 1995, there were no conflicts between the doctors and medical staff in the Zvornik hospital over the treatment of Muslim children. Dr. Ljiljana Vracevic and Dr. Koviljka Gotovac were particularly caring in doing their work. The witness also claims that none of the nurses expressed any religious bad feelings towards the patients. The pediatricians did not have any problems with the nurses either. The witness claims that she would certainly have known if there was any conflict in July 1995 between Dr. Gotovac and the nurses with respect to admitting the little boy to the ward. During October 2007, the witness had a meeting in Zvornik in the hospital in the office of the chief of pediatrics. They met with the Defence team of Drago Nikolic where they discussed the treatment of patients in the Zvornik hospital in July 1995, as well as providing statements about these facts to the Defence team. On that occasion, the witness remembers the conversation, and what Dr. Gotovac said, and she was the doctor who admitted the boy to the ward and treated him in July 1995. Dr. Gotovac said at the time that due to the treatment of Muslim children and the boy, she never had any conflicts with other doctors on that score or with the nurses either. The witness also remembers that Dr. Gotovac confirmed that neither her -- that her family, the Gotovac family never had any unpleasantness because of that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (redacted). I think there was a mistake in the transcript. And my colleague has just drawn my attention to that. In reading the summary at the beginning of the sentence which reads: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: (redacted) I think that I have corrected the mistake in the transcript now. That I read it out properly. That concludes the summary pursuant to the rule, Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Jovicic, does the summary which I've just read out reflect the contents of the statement you gave and the additional statement you made?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does. In full.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The facts contained in the statement, do they say exactly what you would testify about in this Court of law had you been asked about the events?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I'd like to tender the witness statements, the statement of Vela Jovicic, it is 3D472, Exhibit 3D472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few additional questions for this witness before I conclude the examination-in-chief, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Jovicic, in preparing for this testimony, did you look through any hospital documents, and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly did. I looked at all the medical documentation including the history of the -- case history, the patient chart, the letter from the hospital releasing the patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From that documentation, could you determine when you were on duty in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, but may I just take out this piece of paper to remind me of the dates, I prepared them. Dr. Koviljka admitted the boy in the night during the 14th and 15th at 0300 hours. That is to say, the next day. We worked 24 hour shifts. There was just one pediatrician for a 24-hour shift. Now the next day, between the 15th and 16th, Dr. Vracevic came by and she was the head of the children's ward. On the 16th, between the 16th and 17th, I arrived, that is to say, Dr. Jovicic, that's me, and that's when I found the boy there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to show you a photograph which I'd like you to take a look at and tell us who is on the photograph. It is Exhibit P2452, and may we have it displayed on e-court, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, not in public session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the people on the photograph?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Am I allowed to state the name?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, we can move into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the safety we better go into private session, albeit briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you came to the hospital to take up your shift from the previous doctor on duty, what would you talk about, what would you discuss?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: When one doctor took over from another, well, we started at 7 a.m., that's when our shift was, and then we would report orally for each individual patient from one room to the next. And along with this oral reporting, there would be a written report as well, a notebook, in which we recorded everything that had taken place in the last 24 hours. So when a doctor was on duty for 24 hours, he would write a report in this notebook and he would also report orally to the next doctor taking up his shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Apart from that, was other information exchanged with respect to personnel relations at the clinic, in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Interpersonal relations also come within the framework of professional relationships; the relationships between the doctors; the doctors and the nurses; the doctors, nurses and patients; or the parents and relatives of a patient. All that was part of our job, part of the job of the doctor on his 24-hour shift and everything had to be recorded concisely and precisely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And what were your professional relationships like with Dr. Gotovac and Ljiljana Vracevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Jelena Vratovic"]?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: They were professionally good.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'd like to correct something in the transcript. 72, line 9, the name is Ljiljana Vracevic, whereas in the transcript it says Jelena Vratovic. It is Ljiljana Vracevic, L-j-i-l-j-a-n-a V-r-a-c-e-v-i-c. When you took over your duty on that day, the 16th of July, was anything special -- any special information imparted to you with respect to the admission of the boy.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Everything. I was told everything. When he was brought to hospital, when he was admitted, what room he was in, what his health situation was like, who treated him, everything. And we, of course, went to visit the child, the boy. That's what you do when you take over from the previous shift, you take each individual person in turn.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did anyone tell you, the doctor you took over from or anybody else, whether there had been any incidents or whether any of the nurses had attacked and confronted Dr. Gotovac for taking in a Muslim patient?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of those few days in July 1995, did it ever happen that Dr. Koviljka Gotovac complained to you that she had problems because of having (redacted) and treated him, that she had certain problems with any of the nurses?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No, no problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Having in mind your professional relationship as you described it, had there been such an incident, would you have been informed by other doctors, in particular by Dr. Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would have.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Would the then hospital director, Dr. Galic [as interpreted], been informed of that?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, most definitely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In that case, would certain measures have been undertaken against the medical professional?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: A disciplinary procedure is a must in such incident situations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The answer was too quick --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, too quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- for the objection. Shall we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just want to caution my colleague that I think her questions are leading. As to the nature of the objection, I would ask her to refrain from that as she proceeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Again, if you could put a pause between the question and the answer, please. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. At this moment I would kindly ask to move into closed session because of the few next questions I have for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a mistake in the transcript, page 74, line 17. We won't mention any names, Mrs. Jovicic, just a question I have for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you see the gentleman's wife?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I met her by chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, Mrs. Jovicic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the witness's answers since it overlapped with Ms. Nikolic's remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know what she said, probably thank you. Would there be cross-examination by any of the Defence teams? I see none. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I can be brief, I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wondered if my colleagues could be so kind as to give me a copy of the notes that the witness has. I don't know if you were aware that she had them, but I wondered if I might have a copy of them at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Dr. Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My name is Kweku Vanderpuye. On behalf of the Prosecution, I'm going to put some questions to you in respect of your statements and also in respect of your direct examination. If there's any question that I ask you that is unclear to you, right away just let me know and I will try to rephrase it in a way that we can understand each other better, and hopefully this will go a little bit more easily. Now, you met with the Defence, I believe, as recently as yesterday; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to that meeting you discussed what you would be testifying here today about; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you went over the statements that you had previously given; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you also met with the Defence, I believe, on 4th of August, 2007; yes?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You met with them again on the 1st of October, 2007; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't get your answer for the record.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you met with them again on the 21st of March, 2008?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In relation to these three meetings that you had with the Defence, you discussed the subject matter of the statement that you ultimately signed on 23rd March 2008; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And of course before you signed that statement, you had an opportunity to review it carefully?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to remove or change any of its content; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then on the 27th of May in 2008 you signed a second statement; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that was following the 21st March meeting you had with the Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in that second statement, that's the 27th of May, 2008, statement, you recount this meeting that you had with Dr. Gotovac in the office of the chief of the pediatrics ward of the Zvornik hospital; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's in that statement that you say, as you've said today, that Dr. Gotovac made certain comments about her experience treating Muslim children in 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in particular with respect to an incident concerning this nurse; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what is contained -- the information that's contained in your 27th May statement is information that you had when you made the previous statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And so the reason why I'm asking you this question is that if on the 23rd of March, 2008, you already had had this meeting and conversation with Dr. Gotovac, it doesn't appear in that statement and it only appears in your 27th May statement; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is right. Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that because you didn't mention this when you met with the Defence on the 23rd of March or is that because you simply overlooked the fact that it was missing from that statement?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No, everything was public. Everything was told. I don't know how the Defence took note of it. I don't know that. Nothing was hidden, kept were them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Vanderpuye. If Madam Nikolic would take a look at line 21 to 25 of previous page, I was wondering just out of an abundance of caution, did we not deal with this information in private session? Or it is okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I think we dealt with it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll take care of it and let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know how it came to be that this information was put into two separate statements?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke with Ms. Nikolic and other members of her Defence team before the meeting with Dr. Gotovac. I told them then that I had to contact my head first. I was doing my shift for 24 hours, I didn't admit the child. At that time I was employed by the hospital and now I have a contract with them. I had to talk to my head and the doctor who had admitted the child. I can stand by my findings and the information I heard about. I cannot represent here someone else who should speak on their own behalf about their work, and that was my position since day one. I never tried to pose as someone who admitted the child, and right now I only have a contract with the pediatrics ward. I am employed by the health centre. The head nowadays of the pediatrics is Dr. Gotovac. It was Dr. Vracevic who dismissed the child, discharged him from the hospital, and I only had my 24-hour shift during that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, according to your review of the medical records before you came to testify here today, is it your testimony that your shift started on the 16th or on the 17th of July? I think you've got it right there, that note; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. My shift began on the 16th at 700 hours. The 16th in the morning and lasted until the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you don't actually have any firsthand knowledge of the circumstances under which the child was received in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes. No firsthand knowledge, only secondhand. I wasn't witness to it. However, I did keep treating him later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you don't know firsthand circumstances under which he was admitted, who he saw initially?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What his physical condition was at the time that he was received?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is secondhand and even thirdhand information. Dr. Koviljka, Dr. Vracevic and then myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, you are not certain as to when it was that you began your duty until you had an opportunity to review the medical charts; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I'm completely sure of it. However, a lot of time has elapsed and I need to be precise concerning the dates. Our shift began every day at 7 o'clock in the morning. Four pediatricians and each of us would do a 24-hour shift, that's how we rotated. The medical records are there to have some record of the dates. I cannot remember the dates off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that. The reason why I'm asking is because that date doesn't appear in your statement of 23rd March, 2008.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the date doesn't appear in your statement of 27th May 2008.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which suggests to me that you didn't review the medical records between the first time you met the Defence on the 4th August 2007 and October 1st of 2007 or between October 1st 2007 and 21st March of 2008 or between 21st March 2008 and 27th May 2008. So when is it that you decided to look at this medical record?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: The meeting at the ward with the head Dr. Gotovac when Drago Nikolic's team arrived, it is then when we looked at the letters of discharge. And then subsequently, I dug up all of the rest, his case history and everything we had on him. I wanted to be as precise as possible concerning any dates. I recall many things about my work but I didn't have all the dates in my head. That's why it was introduced subsequently. You can check all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. But when exactly did you look up the dates as concerns your own tour of duty, as it were, in July of 1995? When was it that you looked that up, that you checked it?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: As I said, we went through the documentation. At the time we only had the letter of discharge from the pediatrics. Since I no longer worked there. I then asked the director of the hospital and the head of pediatrics to find the rest of the documents in the archives, that was perhaps some 20 days before getting here. I believed I should not appear before the Court without being certain of the facts and the dates so as to be concise and precise. And they met my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I understand that. So you hadn't looked at that information before you signed the statements that are being offered in evidence in this case; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the information that you received concerning -- concerning the events surrounding the reception of this child at the hospital, you say that's based on second, if not thirdhand information; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you would have no independent ability to know whether or not that information was complete; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, you don't have that information and you cannot check. If you have no piece of information, you cannot run your checks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, you don't know if the information is complete or somebody left something out; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I can tell you a hundred per cent certainly that I never heard of any such a thing. No one told me anything like that. I didn't notice anything of that sort. That is what I can tell you and I also was not present there and then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you telling me that as a doctor you've never noticed information in a medical chart that's incomplete? Is that what you are telling me? In all your years as a doctor, you've never seen anything like that?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I do not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm getting at is, if you don't have firsthand information about something, and the only way that you learn about something is if somebody told you, you have no way of knowing whether or not what they've told you is accurate or complete; would you agree with that or you disagree?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot agree with that. I cannot check an information that never reached me. All information pertaining to the boy's condition was of interest me, his mental state, medical situation. There were many foreign delegations there and I frequently gave statements. They even took him out of the hospital at times with my prior approval. I was interested in all that information. However, I never came across any information that would indicate that there had been an incident. Had it been so, had I had that information, I would have checked it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that, Doctor. My point is, if that information weren't recorded, you wouldn't know about it; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you the very same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the fact that it's not recorded doesn't mean it didn't happen; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The fact that it's not recorded, doesn't mean it didn't happen; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, everything I could see on the spot, that is what I can stand by when telling you, but I have never heard of these assumptions and I should not discuss them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm putting to you, I think, a relatively simple, straightforward proposition. The fact that this information was not recorded in a record that you reviewed does not mean that it didn't happen; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: This is all relative. My statement can neither corroborate that nor -- all I can tell you that there was no disciplinary measure instituted, no information. I wasn't present there, and from day one, I was telling the Defence that I wasn't treating the child and that I'm not allowed to give firsthand information. I can only tell you what I did and what the colleagues of mine at the pediatrics ward did while I was there. I did not admit the boy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't understand what the topic is, you are moving on?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am indeed. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you have copies, by the way, of these medical records that you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you have copies of these number of statement that you say that you gave to foreign dignitaries and such that came by the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No, they were fair. On each occasion they paid maximum attention to the boy, they would take him out for a walk, buy him things and then they would return him to the hospital at the scheduled time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I mean is, you mentioned that you had given a number of statements to these people that came by the hospital. I wondered if you had copies of those statements?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You had mentioned that there were individuals, groups that came by the hospital while the child was there; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Those were representatives of international organizations of the International Red Cross, et cetera. And on each occasion, if it was my shift, they asked me if I would allow the boy to go into town for a walk. I didn't even ask my head, I would approve that since I believed it to be the humane way. We cooperated well. They would take him out and return him on time. I have no objections there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you didn't give any statements to these international organizations?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: We talked about it in general about the boy, about his situation, how he is adapting to the newly created conditions, his mental state, his surgical treatment, since it was the surgeons who treated him and we were just providing pediatric care. We discussed such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you mentioned previously that you weren't aware that any disciplinary action had been taken as concerns the treatment of this child; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And that's because the information that you were provided with as concerns what happened surrounding the reception of this child at the hospital, that is, that a nurse apparently became upset and threatened one of the doctors, that would be a matter that should be disciplined; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: If it indeed happened, then absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And would it be also disciplinary -- well, would it also be subject to discipline if a person were to express ethnic intolerance, as it were, with respect to the treatment of a patient?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Absolutely. The head submits a disciplinary report. There is a disciplinary commission -- committee that meets in the presence of the hospital director in case of such incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What if the person just doesn't feel good about doing something based on an ethnic bias? They don't want to perform a given assignment based upon an ethnic bias but they do it in the end. What about that, is that disciplinary, is that subject to discipline?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's not the kind of thing that a person would express knowingly to certainly not a hospital official; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And certainly you are not aware of anybody expressing reluctance to perform a task or an assignment because they just don't feel good about it because they are dealing with Muslims; right? You are not aware of anything like that, are you?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Can you give me a little time and the opportunity to clarify something with respect to Muslim patients, although this might be getting away from the topic, but may I be allowed to say something? I'm speaking in my own name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Now, when it comes to the small boy Adnan, he is the boy who came to our ward before the war and he remained there because his parents had divorced. His mother never appeared so we treated him as our child. We loved him so much that when we didn't have -- hardly had anything to eat, we would celebrate his birthday, make a birthday cake and things like that. I took him to the sea side with Zijo, another boy, and I was the only person crying because Adnan put his arms around me and he said, Don't let me go. We loved him. The other mothers didn't cry but I did. And the other boy too, we loved him. And every time I would see him, I would love to take him home to make him some nice lunch, give him some money. So I'm speaking in my own personal name. But the other doctors did, Dr. Vracevic and Stamenkovic and Dr. Koviljka too, we were very much attached to the child. You know, when somebody grows up there in front of you, you love somebody very much. Perhaps sometimes even more than your own children, if I can say that. But that is the humane kind of feelings one feels. So I came to the children's ward in 1993 and there were children there when I arrived. They were all taken care of, they were all exchanged and linked up with their families. I don't want to hold a lecture here but the children's ward, I'm not talking about other wards, but the children's ward was an exemplary ward of how one should care for patients and people in general during the war and was a good example to people and to nurses that there must never be any ethnic bias or any other bias. So I'd like to say this and -- so that people can hear my opinion and how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have 65 ter 02482B in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we haven't received a list of the documents that my learned friend wishes to use during the cross-examination of this witness. So may we be provided by the document -- with the document. And Mr. Ogrizovic is checking his e-mail but it doesn't appear that we received anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We have been addressing that issue just now, Mr. President, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, we have Gavric's statement in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could just go to the second page, it's ERN ending 2937. In particular, Dr. Jovicic, I want to just refer you to paragraph 4 of this statement. This is a statement that was given by Dr. Gavric in relation to his involvement with certain Muslim prisoners, patients. And he says in paragraph 4 that in relation to that he made a request to the chief nurse for two nurses to assist in the transport of the patients from Milici to Zvornik hospital. He says, "However, two were not available and only one nurse accompanied me." And he says, "This nurse mentioned that she did not 'feel good' about the assignment since her brother had been killed during the war." Now, it appears that she actually did perform this assignment, but is that kind of behaviour the type of behaviour you observed in the hospital, because she is addressing the director of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Not on my ward. And that deserves to be criticized, that kind of behaviour. Deserves condemnation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You know that that child, when he arrived first at the hospital, didn't go directly to your ward now, don't you?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it went to the emergency ward first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he dealt with nurses at that emergency ward that might not actually be working where you work; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it also occurs to me that having seen this in a statement of the director of the hospital, that this actually might not be all that sanctionable, do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Not fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. When you reviewed the documents in relation to the receipt -- reception, I should say, of this child at the hospital, did you learn at any time that he had survived a mass execution along with his father?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: I received information that he was found in a forest and had experienced a trauma. It was terrible. It was a trauma for this small child to have lived through something like that and then to have been found in a forest, so that was the information that the doctor had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I misspoke in my question. His father was actually executed. Did you find that information concerning the trauma that this child went through and being found in a forest in a medical record?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Well, it's like this, since I am a doctor who worked there at the time and that he was in our hospital for six months, the trauma was noticeable. I wasn't there on the first day, but on the second and third day, I could see that the child had been traumatized and it was quite natural that that should have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you find in the records that he reviewed that he was found in a forest?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That's what I was told orally, and that's what was written in the child case history as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you told orally what doctor he first saw when he went there, on the surgical ward, were you told what doctor he saw?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Dr. Lazarevic was called to the emergency ward. They don't have a children's surgical department but he treated him surgically. Then it was agreed that the child would spend his time in the children's ward because it was a more pleasant atmosphere and that they would come and take him to surgery whenever necessary. And when his condition improved, his wounds were seen to at the children's ward. They didn't have to take him away to the surgical ward to do that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. In relation to your conversation with Dr. Gotovac in October of 2007, you said that she indicated that she suffered no problems as a result of having treated this child; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And she also indicated that --

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: She also indicated that her family had suffered no problems as a result of her having treated this child; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And in fact, you said that she intended to make a statement to that effect; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in fact she didn't make any written statement to that effect; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: That is right because she changed her mind subsequently and the reasons given were for family reasons, which she didn't want to disclose, and we didn't insist upon that. We didn't think we had the right to infringe upon her privacy so that's something she said later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say "we" who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, there was the Defence of Mr. Nikolic and I was there too. However, when they came back again she said that she had changed her mind due to family reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And the two of you are not close friends; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: We just have a professional relationship that's a good relationship but not privately, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't share any kinds of private issues amongst yourself; right?

utterances.speaker: VELA JOVICIC
utterances.text: Not private, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just bear with me for one moment, Mr. President. Thank you very much, Dr. Jovicic. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, you have any redirect.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do have a few questions for this witness but it seems that we are just two minutes before the end of the session. And since the cross-examination of the Prosecution lasted much longer than they indicated, I'd like to look through the transcript and leave my few questions for tomorrow, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just want to alert the Court that I believe our estimate was an hour for this witness and I think I've done better than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, I wonder whether you can finish in 5 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that would be -- would not be possible, Your Honour. Even with the best will in the world.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have to ask then whether Doctor would be available tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If need be then, yes, what can I do. I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There seems no other way. Then we'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of September, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.43 p.m.,
